lesson.menu_title: What They Said in the Meeting
lesson.menu_desc: Reported speech and reporting verbs: the decision, the objection and the next step, told to a third person
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 9 -- What They Said in the Meeting
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Amanda Merlini | Lesson 9 -- What They Said in the Meeting

vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: to mention something briefly, so that it is on the record
to tell somebody about a risk before it happens
to say something clearly and formally, as a fact
to tell somebody what you think they should do
to accept that something is true, even when you do not like it
to draw attention to a fact that the others may have missed
to say that something is true or will happen, after checking
to give reasons to show that your position is right

items.situation: Karin asks: "What did the buyer want?"
tips: Their lawyer stated that they wanted two hundred thousand credits.
want becomes wanted: one step back.

items.situation: She asks: "Did the verifier say the annex was fine?"
tips: He confirmed that the annex had arrived.

items.situation: She asks: "What was our finance director worried about?"
tips: He warned that the price might fall before the spring.

items.situation: She asks: "And what did you tell them?"
tips: I advised them to link the payment to the issuance, not to a date.

items.situation: She asks: "Did they accept that the market is moving?"
tips: Their lawyer acknowledged that the market was moving, but she did not change her position.
acknowledge: she admitted a point she did not like.

items.situation: She asks: "When is the draft coming?"
tips: They said they would send it by Friday.

listenings.text: Before we close, let me summarize where we are, so that nobody leaves with a different version. First, the decision. We agree in principle to buy two hundred thousand credits from the Serra Verde project, subject to verification. Second, the objection. Your finance director has argued that a fixed price exposes you if the market falls, and I have noted that. Our position has not changed. We need a fixed price, because our board approves budgets a year in advance. Third, the next step. Amanda has proposed linking the payment to the date the credits are issued, instead of a calendar date. I think that could work, but I cannot confirm it today. We will send a draft clause by Friday, and I would ask you to send your comments within a week. If anyone remembers this differently, please say so now.

When you report what somebody said in a meeting, the verb you choose is not a detail. It is a decision, and the reader will trust it. Said is neutral, and neutral is often the safest choice. But the other verbs carry information. If you write that the other side argued something, you are telling the reader that they gave reasons and that somebody disagreed. If you write that they acknowledged something, you are saying they accepted a point they did not like, and that is useful to know. And then there is claimed. Claimed means you are not sure the statement is true. In your own notes that may be fine. In an email that the other side will read, it is close to an accusation. So before you send the summary, read only the verbs. If the verbs tell a story that you would not say out loud in the room, change them.

extra_audio.text: Start by saying which meeting it was, and who was there. Then report the decision. Then report the objection, and who raised it. Then report the next step, and who owns it. And finally, say what is still open.
